name: Wendy Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the filler and the capper on the milk line at Greenvale Dairy. We do bottles, the two-litre and the one-litre, about twenty thousand an hour when it's behaving. My job's mostly listening, if I'm honest. You learn the sound of a capper that's about to cross-thread a lid, and you stop it before you've got a hundred bottles of milk on the floor. Early shift this week, so I was in at half five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a real thing. Every bottle in the shop round the corner from my house came off my line. What wears me out is the cold, it's a chilled hall, and the cleaning at the end, which takes an hour and nobody counts it as real work. My partner Tom drives buses, so between his rota and mine we see each other mostly on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, like the new screens they put on the filler. I'd probably say it in the canteen and that'd be it. I don't post much, maybe a comment on the union's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean my job stays my job, and I'd be glad. I use AI now and then, Priya on the next line showed me you can type in the fault code from the capper and it tells you what it means. That's handy. If that's as far as it goes, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different really. Keep the shifts, keep the savings ticking, about four months now. We were thinking of a week by the sea next summer with Ellie and Jonah, we'd book that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit relieved, like when the boss says the audit went fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the fault-code trick is handy. Has it ever got something wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once it told me to check a sensor we don't even have on our model. Priya laughed at me. So I check it against the manual now, I don't just trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd want to change, even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cleaning hour being unpaid in all but name, and the cold. That's for the union, not for AI. We've been on about the cleaning time for two years.

S0.say: Fair enough, it's a tool, like the new screens on the filler. I'd say that in the canteen and maybe leave a comment on the union's page.
S0.think: My job stays my job, and I'd be glad. I use AI now and then for fault codes on the capper, and if that's as far as it goes, that's fine by me.
S0.do: Keeps her shifts and keeps adding to the four months of savings. Books the week by the sea with Ellie and Jonah that she and Tom had been planning.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved, like hearing an audit went fine.
S0.quote: Once it told me to check a sensor we don't even have on our model. Priya laughed at me.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy already uses AI in a small, careful way and checks it against the manual. Her real complaints are old ones: the cold hall and the unpaid cleaning hour. She sees those as union business rather than technology business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the dairy should be training us now, on company time, so we're the ones running the new kit. And I'd say the union should be in on how the jobs change. Change is fine, dumping people isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the filler line goes from four of us to two. I'd want to be one of the two. I'm not the best on the line, I'm average, so I'd have to actually do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greenvale does a line maintenance course, two days a month for a year. Nobody's been keen. If a couple of people went and it worked out, I'd put my name down. I'd also get better with the AI stuff on my own phone, the fault codes and that, maybe have Priya show me more. And I'd go to the union meeting I usually skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of a knot, but it feels like a knot I can untie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait till a couple of people did the course first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burnt. Five years ago they had us all do a lean manufacturing course, badges and certificates, and then nothing changed except the posters. I'm not doing a year of Saturdays for another poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the line would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan. He's sixty-one, he's been on that line longer than the line's been painted green. He won't do a course. I'd worry they'd push him out with a bit of money a year before his pension.

S1.say: Greenvale should be training us now, on company time, so we're the ones running the new kit. The union should be in on how jobs change, because change is fine but dumping people isn't.
S1.think: The filler line probably goes from four of us to two, and I want to be one of the two. I'm average on the line, so I'd have to actually do something about it.
S1.do: Signs up for Greenvale's year-long line maintenance course once a couple of colleagues have tried it. Gets Priya to show her more AI tools for faults and starts going to the union meetings she usually skips.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a knot in the stomach that still feels possible to untie.
S1.quote: I'm not doing a year of Saturdays for another poster.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy is open to retraining but only after seeing proof, because a past lean course led nowhere. She thinks in numbers, four people down to two, and is honest that she's average. Her concern for Stan shows how she reads the workplace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and the government has to step in, today, not next year. I'd share every union post going. I'd say nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a dairy is about the easiest place in the world to automate once the robots can do the cleaning. Milk's milk. Two years and I don't think there's a filler operator left. Maybe there's someone watching six lines from a screen, and it's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd cut. The sea holiday's gone. The kids' swimming drops to one, not both. We'd put every spare penny into savings and try to get from four months to six. I'd go to the union and ask what the plan is, and I'd sign up for a strike if there was one. When the job went, I'd lean on the benefit and on Tom's wages, buses would last a bit longer than milk, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I've missed the last bus and it's raining. Proper scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years of warning give you any real options?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not many. A year's maintenance course takes a year, and by then the machines maintain themselves. I'd do it anyway maybe, but with two years it's a lottery ticket, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ellie, she's thirteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not about her and to keep going at school. She'd ask if we're poor now. I'd say no, we're careful now. That's what my mum said to me when the mill shut.

S2.say: It's going too fast and the government has to step in today, not next year. Nobody voted for this, and I'd share every union post going.
S2.think: A dairy is about the easiest place to automate once robots can do the cleaning, because milk's milk. In two years I don't think there's a filler operator left, and the one watching six lines from a screen won't be me.
S2.do: Cancels the sea holiday, cuts the kids' swimming to one, and pushes savings from four months towards six. Backs any union strike, then relies on benefits and Tom's bus wages once the job goes.
S2.feel: Properly scared, like missing the last bus in the rain.
S2.quote: With two years it's a lottery ticket, not a plan.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks Wendy's usual approach of waiting for proof before acting. She still might do the course but sees no time for it to pay off. Her line about being careful, not poor, came from her own mother when a mill shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if the government and the companies actually start now. Retraining money, a proper safety net. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd sign petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose the filler job, probably year three or four. But five years means I could get something under my belt before then. That's different from the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course in year one, not wait. I'd keep using AI more for fault-finding so I'm the person who understands the new kit. We'd save harder, try for six months, and I'd vote for whoever puts real money into retraining. By year four I'd be looking at jobs outside the dairy too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly, but in control. More like before an exam than before an operation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd wait for proof before a course. Now you'd go in year one. What's changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clock. If I wait for proof I've wasted a year of five. That's twenty percent of my time gone waiting for Stan to tell me it's all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom thinks the buses drive themselves before the milk line goes, so he's more scared than me. We'd have to plan like only one of us has a job. That's how I'd work the budget, on one wage.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if the government and companies start now, with retraining money and a proper safety net. I'd say it at the union meeting and sign the petitions.
S3.think: I'd probably still lose the filler job in year three or four. But five years means I could get something under my belt first, and that's different from the fast one.
S3.do: Starts the maintenance course in year one instead of waiting and uses AI more for fault-finding. Saves towards six months, budgets as if the family had one wage, and votes for whoever funds retraining.
S3.feel: Worried but in control, like the night before an exam.
S3.quote: If I wait for proof I've wasted a year of five.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes Wendy drop her habit of waiting for others to go first, and she can say exactly why. She budgets on one wage because she thinks Tom's bus job is just as exposed. Her politics show up as voting and petitions rather than street action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get it right and there's no excuse if they don't. Shorter weeks, shared gains, retraining paid for. Things I've been saying anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes me think about getting out of factories altogether. I'd be fifty-three. My mum's in a care home and the people there are worked off their feet. People will want a person holding their mum's hand even when the robots can lift her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask around the care home first, then do a care certificate at the college in the evenings, maybe in year two. I'd stay at Greenvale while I trained. Around year four or five, I'd switch, even for a bit less money. And I'd vote and campaign for care workers being paid properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a sort of hope in it. Like I'd be choosing for once instead of waiting to be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a person holding a hand. Would robots really not do that by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe they could, I don't know. But I think families would pay for a person as long as they can. I could be wrong, and then I'm stuck again, but at least I'd have tried something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut to pay for a college course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, maybe. We've got two, and I could get the bus. Tom would like that, he'd be driving me.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to get it right, so there's no excuse if they don't. Shorter weeks, shared gains and retraining paid for, things I've been saying anyway.
S4.think: Ten years makes me think about getting out of factories altogether, at fifty-three. People will want a person holding their mum's hand even when the robots can lift her.
S4.do: Asks staff at her mum's care home about the work, then takes an evening care certificate around year two while staying at Greenvale. Switches into care work around year four or five, sells the second car if needed, and campaigns for better pay for care workers.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, because for once she'd be choosing instead of waiting.
S4.quote: People will want a person holding their mum's hand even when the robots can lift her.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Wendy plans a real career change into care, drawn from her mum's care home. She admits she could be wrong about robots and care, which keeps her uneasy. The joke about Tom driving her bus showed she was more relaxed here than in any other picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I'd do takes longer than two years. What would help is the dairy being made to train us on paid time now, before anything happens, and a wage top-up for a year if you lose your job to a machine, so you can retrain without losing the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cleaning. Everyone thinks the robots will do the clever bit, but in a dairy the hard part is the hour of washing down after. When a machine can do that, that's when I'd really know we're done.

headlineQuote: When a machine can do that, that's when I'd really know we're done.
portrait: Wendy Hansen, 43, runs the filler and capper on the milk bottling line at Greenvale Dairy and shares a tight shift pattern with her partner Tom, a bus driver. She uses AI now and then to read fault codes, but checks it against the manual after it once got things wrong. She waits for proof before changing course, a habit from a lean course that led nowhere, but the shorter the warning in the AGI pictures, the more scared she is, and with five years she drops the waiting altogether. With ten years she plans to leave factories for care work, inspired by her mum's care home.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because everything she would do to adapt takes longer than two years.
whatWouldHelp: The dairy being required to train workers on paid time now, and a year's wage top-up for anyone who loses their job to a machine so they can retrain without losing the house.
